description: Brooks's 'best bull reversal bar': the minimum reversal-bar test plus at least M of the open/tail/overlap quality sub-tests. An M-of-N score, not an AND.

complexity.reason: an M-of-N count over otherwise trivial sub-tests; each sub-test is cheap but the scoring shape is new to the corpus

merge_notes: Carried as a composite under the named-Brooks-setup exception: 'the best bull reversal bars have more than one of the following' is the book's own scoring statement, and an M-of-N count is not reachable by ANDing panes. Graded by its hardest part, which is the count itself. The source also folds in a follow-through-bar term; that is dropped with V00-34 as a look-ahead condition.

description: Each of the last N bars is a bull trend bar AND barely overlaps the bar before it (each bar's low is no more than X ticks below the previous bar's low): a Brooks spike with little overlap.
pseudocode: for k in 0..spikeBars-1: close[k] > open[k] && (close[k] - open[k]) >= bodyFraction * (high[k] - low[k]) && (k == spikeBars-1 || low[k] >= low[k+1] - maxOverlapTicks * tickSize)

complexity.reason: a fixed-length loop combining a per-bar classification with a bar-to-bar overlap test inside the run

merge_notes: V19-03 is V19-02 with spikeBars fixed at 2 plus a first-hour session gate; merged as a fixed parameter, and the session gate is dropped (it is TimeWindow from the catalog, ANDed in a separate pane). Kept apart from ConsecutiveTrendBars because the pairwise overlap term applies between adjacent bars of the run and cannot be ANDed in from another pane. Brooks's spikeBars: 2 for a light always-in read, 3-4 for a trend-day read; default 3.

description: A small-range bar that closes up and whose low is within X ticks of the lowest low of the last N bars (short: mirrored) - the small bar shows the sellers have stopped at that level.
pseudocode: (high[0] - low[0]) <= smallFraction * atr(atrLookback) && low[0] <= lowest(low, extremeLookback)[1] + nearTicks * tickSize && close[0] > open[0]

complexity.reason: an ATR window and a Lowest window, plus a proximity test on the current bar

catalog_match.note: CloseNearPriorLow measures the CLOSE against the single previous bar's low plus an offset; this measures the LOW against the lowest low of a window. Different bars.

merge_notes: Two of its three terms are carried elsewhere (BarRangeAboveAtrMultiple negated, TrendBarBody at bodyFraction 0), but the proximity-to-a-recent-extreme term is not carried anywhere in this bucket, so the setup is kept whole rather than dropped as a composition. Brooks's actual test is a visual comparison against 'a big bar'; the window low is the mechanizable reading.

description: A price gap left behind by a breakout is a magnet: the market is drawn back to fill or retest the gap's near edge, which serves as a target for a position taken away from it.
pseudocode: gapLevel = low[g] where low[g] > high[g + 1]; low[0] <= gapLevel + toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: the gap's boundary must persist from the bar where it formed

merge_notes: Same level test in three books. R10-09 states the magnet tendency generally (a true bar gap or a moving-average gap bar); V01-13 states it as an intraday context filter on a tracked breakout/measuring gap, so the same rule in the Entry role; T22-08 uses it as the cover target for a fade, with the gap being the two or three trend bars that carried price between two trading ranges (a band rather than a single level, hence the tolerance). Recorded as an Exit because two of three sources use it as a target; the authoring pass can place the same condition as an Entry filter.

description: A gap up is followed within a few bars by a gap down whose range does not overlap the first gap (an island top); enter or hold short on a retest of the island's bottom.
pseudocode: gap1 at i: low[i] > high[i + 1]; gap2 at j (j < i, i - j <= maxIslandBars): high[j] < low[j + 1] && low[j + 1] > high[i]; islandBottom = high[j]; high[0] <= islandBottom + toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: two remembered gap events plus a non-overlap test between them, persisting across the island's width

merge_notes: Kept apart from GapLevelRetest: that needs one gap, this needs a matched pair with a non-overlap constraint, so it fires on a small subset of the same bars.

description: The prior bar poked no more than X ticks above the highest high of the bars before it and this bar has closed back below that level — a failed marginal breakout, traded in the reversal direction.
pseudocode: level = highest(high, lookback)[2]; high[1] > level && high[1] - level <= barelyTicks * (MinMove / PriceScale) && close[0] < level

complexity.reason: an EL Highest read at a two-bar offset, plus two comparisons; Max Bars Back must cover lookback + 2

catalog_match.note: No catalog rule tests a failed breakout.

merge_notes: R02-26 ('breaks a resistance level by only a tick or so and then reverses down') and R02-27 ('barely breaks one level but pulls back before reaching the next one that is just a little higher') are one behaviour: the breakout bar cleared the nearest level by almost nothing and price is back under it. R02-27's second, higher level cannot be mechanized without a set of remembered pivots (see the resistance-level design decision) and adds nothing on a fixed-window level, since not reaching a higher level is implied by reversing back under the lower one. Level taken as Highest(High, N)[2] — the extreme of the bars BEFORE the poking bar. B rather than A: it is a three-way test across three bar offsets and the [2]-offset Highest is easy to get wrong, but the definition itself is unambiguous.

description: After a session opening gap up, the next bar trades at least one tick below the gap bar's low, back into the gap — a fade signal; mirrored after a gap down.

complexity.reason: one-tick offset test on top of the session-gap primitive

merge_notes: Three statements of the same glossary definition. T00-11 and V00-17's fixed prior-bar form won over R00-25's 'low of the session's first bar', which would need the first bar remembered across the day. V00-17 arrived as a stray from bar_anatomy_reversal_signal.

description: The book's named major-trend-reversal setup, kept whole because Brian would want to test it as Brooks states it: a strong trend-line break, then a failed test of the trend's extreme, then a strong reversal signal bar on that test.

complexity.reason: graded by its hardest part, the trend-line break and projection

catalog_match.note: the mining files list a likely_existing_rule of MajorTrendReversal, but no such rule is in rules/CATALOG.md -- it does not exist yet

merge_notes: One of the named Brooks setups MERGE.md keeps as a composite. V24-14 is the mechanizable statement and supplies the parameters; V03-06 is the chapter's four-part definition, whose items 1-3 are the same three parts. V03-06's item 4 ('the second reversal goes far enough for a consensus that the trend has reversed') is DROPPED, not parameterized: Brooks gives no number, the mining file flags it as out of scope for a bar-level test, and inventing a consensus threshold would put the whole setup at C for no gain. With item 4 gone every part is measurable and the rule grades B. Its parts live in lines_channels_trendlines (TrendLineBreak, ExtremeTestAfterTrendLineBreak) and bar_anatomy_reversal_signal (the signal bar).

description: When the bar that produced the entry had a range smaller than K x ATR — a weak, slow break rather than a decisive one — cap the trade at a scalp target instead of holding for a swing.
pseudocode:
entryBarRange = the high-low range of the bar at BarsSinceEntry bars back;
entryBarRange < minBreakAtrMultiple * atr(atrLookback) && ctx.OpenPositionProfit() >= scalpTicks * tickSize * bigPointValue

complexity.reason: needs the entry bar's range carried forward through the trade, then an ATR comparison and a profit test

catalog_match.note: AtrProfitTarget always exits at K x ATR of profit; this exits at a FIXED tick target but only when the entry bar was small, so it is a conditional target, not a scaled one

merge_notes: The candidate anchors on 'the trend-line break bar', which would need the line machinery; re-anchored on the ENTRY bar, which the engine already knows and which is the same bar in the setup Brooks describes. That substitution is what makes it authorable at all.

description: Exit the long when the high reaches the range-height measured move -- the top of the prior N-bar range plus that range's own height (mirrored for the short). Brooks's standard trading-range target.
pseudocode: rangeHigh = highest(high, rangeLookback)[1]; rangeLow = lowest(low, rangeLookback)[1]; target = rangeHigh + (rangeHigh - rangeLow); high[0] >= target - toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: the stateless rolling form is two window extremes; the book's form freezes the projection at the breakout bar, which would need a persistent variable

catalog_match.note: Both are computed targets, but AtrProfitTarget scales open profit by ATR and never looks at where the range was; this projects a price from the window's own height.

merge_notes: The stateless rolling form is taken over the book's frozen-at-the-breakout form, on the merge brief's most-mechanizable rule; R08-13's own notes propose exactly that simplification. The rolling target drifts as the window rolls, which is the cost -- flagged for the authoring pass. Brooks's own caveat is that the exact distance is only approximate however it is measured.

description: The current signal bar's entry price is at or above the first signal bar's (mirror: at or below) - Brooks's trap test on a second entry: 'if the second entry is letting you in at a better price than the first, be suspicious. Most good second entries are at the same price or worse.'
pseudocode: high[0] >= high[firstSignalBarIndex] - toleranceTicks * tickSize   // firstSignalBarIndex from the SecondSignal scan

complexity.reason: reuses SecondSignal's scan and compares one retained price

merge_notes: Single source, kept as its own rule rather than folded into SecondSignal because it is a separate, independently meaningful test and Brooks states it as an override ('good fill, bad trade'); a placement can want the second entry without the price gate. It cannot be authored before SecondSignal, since it reads the same scan's first-signal bar. Figure 10.1's bar 10 is the book's counter-example: one tick better than bar 9, and it failed.

description: Exit a high-N long (low-N short) as soon as price trades back below the count's signal bar low (above its high) before the position has reached a scalper's profit. Brooks: 'if the market reverses and trades below the low of the pattern before reaching at least a scalper's profit, the high 2 buy has failed.'
pseudocode: ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && low[0] < signalLow && ctx.OpenPositionProfit() < scalpProfitTicks * tickSize * bigPointValue

complexity.reason: reads HighLowBarCount's retained signalLow plus open-profit state

catalog_match.note: a stop at a PATTERN price (the signal bar's low) gated on not yet having made a scalper's profit, not a fixed dollar loss

merge_notes: Single source, and an Exit, so it cannot be reached by placing FailedCountReversal in the exit pane (an Entry cannot sit there - the catalog makes the same call for ConsecutiveCloseExit). Same event as FailedCountReversal, opposite use: that one takes the other side, this one just gets out. R17-12's own note is worth keeping: a failed count usually becomes the next count number, which is simply HighLowBarCount continuing to advance, so no separate rule is needed for 'a failed high 2 becomes a high 3'.
